speechtext: It being five o'clock the house will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely, notices of motion and public bills.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PREVENT DISTRIBUTION OF MISLEADING INFORMATION
REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PREVENT DISTRIBUTION OF MISLEADING INFORMATION
speechtext:
That a special committee be appointed to carry out a survey of all aspects of commercial advertising on Canadian television and radio, in certain newspapers and other fields of mass communication, for the purpose of recommending what steps, if any, should be taken to prevent the distribution of fraudulent and misleading advertising to Canadian consumers;
That the said committee consist of fifteen members to be named at a later date, nine of whom shall constitute a quorum;
That the said committee be empowered to send for persons, papers and records; to sit while the house is sitting; to report from time to time; and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee and that standing order 66 be suspended in relation thereto.
He said: Mr. Speaker, while the majority of advertisers, manufacturers and retailers are completely and entirely ethical in this country,

there are still far too many who are selling rubbish by false suggestion, by half-truths, and by words carefully chosen to mean nothing when they are challenged in a court of law. If, for example, we take an old magazine, let us say one of 50 years or so ago, the advertisements in them seem ridiculous to us; I refer to the advertisements and the claims that are made therein. However, somehow or other, we do not seem to feel this way about a current magazine, a television commercial or a radio spot. Many of them are just an insult to our intelligence.
In the dark ages of the art, advertising literally got away with murder. According to history, it was not unknown for an advertiser to exploit a nostrum offering to stop a baby's crying. Apparently that claim was valid for, after swallowing certain of these concoctions, some babies never cried again. Various rugged individuals were induced by advertising to search for symptoms of dire diseases. Sick folks were persuaded to trifle with major maladies. Consumers were educated to consume nonsensical compounds or deadly poisons or habit forming drugs.
Then, as now, the bulk of Canadian business was sound and reputable. Interspersed were the pirates. Some of these freebooters used advertising to further outrageous exploitation of their victims. Such advertising ran all the way from murder, manslaughter and other crimes through felony and misdemeanor to misrepresentation and misleading tricks. However, actually these old ruffians became playful at times. There is the legendary figure of the advertiser who offered at some alluring price "complete sewing machine, all charges prepaid" for $3.95. When the victim received an envelope in return for his money, if he did not open it very carefully he got stuck a second time, for in the envelope was a needle. That was the complete sewing machine.
When business became slack, it was stimulated by fresh offers. If legend is correct, there was the advertising of "Beautifully framed: Genuine steel engraving of Queen Victoria for only a dollar." What the sucker in this case received was a postage stamp. It was a steel engraving; it was Queen Victoria, but the one who got beautifully framed was the purchaser himself. I think perhaps I may be pardoned if I mention another illustration. We all know the old story. Years ago there was advertised a complete killer of potato bugs for $1. It was stated that if you sent $1 in you would get the necessary ingredients to kill all the potato bugs in a 10-acre field. What you received when the parcel came were two blocks of wood with the instructions that, of course, if you placed a potato bug between the two blocks, they
Request jor Commercial Advertising Survey certainly would kill that potato bug and all the rest, as well. That is an old story and it is supposedly true.
Today the majority of advertisers-and I cannot stress this enough-are high grade organizations of responsibility and integrity. In its lower fringes, however, advertising is still smeared with much that is definitely unfriendly to consumers. Periodically the shysters get too bold. There are "crime waves" in advertising as there are in other activities. Fraudulent and misleading advertising shatters the public's confidence in publicity. Consumers then become less responsive to all advertising. Apparently there will long be a continued need for clean-up campaigns to give the truth-in-advertising movement another forward surge. Fortunately, much of the ground thus gained is held. The long pull trend of advertising honesty appears to be gradually upward. Therefore, a discussion of misrepresentation in advertising should not -and I hope that my remarks will make this clear-smear advertising as a whole. Consumers can help both themselves and reputable business by continuing to use their influence against shysters.
Today in this country one of the most active groups is the Canadian association of consumers, a group of women who are banded together across all of Canada, and who are trying to protect the consumer in so many different ways. I have had a number of discussions with their president, Mrs. Plumptre, here in Ottawa, and others who have pointed out various attempts by advertisers to mislead.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PREVENT DISTRIBUTION OF MISLEADING INFORMATION
speechtext: Such as sliced bacon camouflaging.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PREVENT DISTRIBUTION OF MISLEADING INFORMATION
speechtext:
Yes. That is the kind of thing referred to. What legislation have we now? First of all, there is the Combines Investigation Act, section 33C (1) which reads as follows:
(1)	Everyone who, for the purpose of promoting the sale or use of an article, makes any materially misleading representation to the public, by any means whatever, concerning the price-
And I stress again "the price".
*-at which such or like articles have been, are, or will be, ordinarily sold is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
But again, Mr. Chairman, please listen to this. Subsection 2 reads as follows:
(2)	Subsection (1) does not apply to a person who publishes an advertisement that he accepts in good faith for publication in the ordinary course of his business.
This particular section of the Combines Investigation Act was recently tested in Toronto. I am sure that hon. members recall the case very well as it was the first case in which a firm by the name of Eddy Black was

Request for Commercial Advertising Survey prosecuted under nine counts of misrepresentation as to price, was convicted under nine counts and fined. The magistrate at that particular point said that the reason the fines were not heavier was that it was the first testing of the law. In fairness I must say that the company has indicated that they may appeal. I am not sure whether they have done so. However, the Combines Investigation Act refers only to price, and this idea, of course, where they advertise a selling price of $5 and that the suggested retail price is $15 but the article is really worth only $5 in the final analysis.
The Criminal Code, section 306, is also pertinent. It reads as follows:
(1)	Everyone who publishes or causes to be published an advertisement containing a statement that purports to be a statement of fact but that is untrue, deceptive or misleading or is intentionally so worded or arranged that it is deceptive or misleading, is guilty of an indictable offence-
Subsection 2 states as follows:
(2)	Everyone who publishes or causes to be published in an advertisement a statement or guarantee of the performance, efficacy or length of life of anything that is not based upon an adequate and proper test of that thing, the proof of which lies upon the accused, is, if the advertisement is published to promote, directly or indirectly, the sale or disposal of that thing, guilty of an offence-
But again subsections 1 and 2 do not apply to a person who publishes an advertisement that he accepts in good faith for publication in the ordinary course of business.
Finally, as to legislation, we have the Food and Drugs Act. A very fine article was published within this last few months in the 1961 Canada Year Book. The article was written by Dr. C. A. Morrell, director, food and drug directorate, Department of National Health and Welfare, Ottawa. I should like to quote some things he said because it seems to me they are extremely pertinent.
The present Food and Drugs Act is a federal statute with provisions applying to the manufacture, advertising, packaging-and this is what we are discussing now-sale of food, drugs, cosmetics and medical devices anywhere in Canada. There are no similar provincial laws. It seems to me that is one of the weaknesses in our system as to legislation.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PREVENT DISTRIBUTION OF MISLEADING INFORMATION
speechtext: They have no jurisdiction in criminal affairs.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PREVENT DISTRIBUTION OF MISLEADING INFORMATION
speechtext:
That is so. This federal law exists for the protection of the consumer. Food and drug legislation of some kind has been known in the world for centuries. The first Canadian law of general scope was "An Act to Impose Licence Duties on the Compounders of Spirits and to Prevent the Adulteration of Food, Drink and Drugs". It was passed in May 1874 and became effective

on January 1, 1875. In this act the present Food and Drugs Act had its origin. There have been many minor and several major amendments to the law since 1874, the most recent one being passed in 1953. The original law was the first such law of national scope in North America, and there has been continuous enforcement since 1875.
Here are the powers and scope of the national Food and Drugs Act. There is authority provided (1) to establish standards of composition or identity for foods, drugs and cosmetics; (2) to prohibit the sale of foods that are dirty or harmful; (3) to prohibit the sale of drugs manufactured under unsanitary conditions or that are adulterated; (4) to provide standards for all drugs; (5) to require licences for certain biological preparations; (6) to prohibit the sale of harmful cosmetics or those made under unsanitary conditions; (7) to prohibit the sale of harmful medical devices and, (8)-this to my mind is a very important one-to prohibit the advertising, labelling, packaging or processing of foods or drugs "in a manner that is false, misleading or deceptive or is likely to create an erroneous impression regarding its character, value, quantity" and so on.
The act has a clause that prohibits the advertising of any food, drug or cosmetic to the general public as a treatment, preventative or cure for a number of serious diseases and also lists drugs that may be sold only on prescription.
The Food and Drugs Act is a part of criminal law and it lays down standards and other requirements that will minimize health hazards and fraud in the sale and use of these products. It outlines areas of responsibilities for the manufacturers and distributors but it does not guarantee that drugs will meet the quality standards that are expected of them.
The Food and Drugs Act contains clauses and sections with respect to advertising. It is illegal to make false, exaggerated or misleading claims about a drug or to create an erroneous impression as to its composition, character, value, quantity, merit or safety. The work of enforcing this section is considerable since the advertising of drugs is very extensive. Control of advertising is limited to that directed at the general public.
With all these factors in the legislation you may ask whether we are not protected sufficiently. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we do have adequate legislation. I am not a lawyer by profession and perhaps not as well versed in the statutes of our country as some of our legal members, but it seems to me that we do not have the necessary

regulations. There are a number of other members who wish to speak and perhaps they will be able to deal with that aspect.
The other day when the postmaster general of the United States was here he held a press conference. He was asked about the problem of advertising by means of television and radio. Evidently they have the same problem in the United States that we have here. I have complained many times about the fact that we are flooded with television advertising from the United States, much of which seems to me to be in bad taste, much of which seems to be misleading. In some cases the advertising in their magazines is terrible. We do not hear so much about radio advertising in the United States perhaps because we do not listen to their stations.

speechtext: Oh, yes, we do. The C.B.C. takes it in big quantities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to discuss two or three cases that are very much in point. One is the recent Colgate-Palmolive case in the United States. In their television advertising the shaving of sandpaper was depicted. I will not discuss that further. I know that my seatmate, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave), would like to discuss that one. He has had experience in the fields of radio and journalism, and this is a very interesting case.
I might point out the difference with regard to control between Canada and the United States. In the United States the policing body is the federal trade commission, and under the Clayton act and its amendments it seems to me they are doing a magnificent job. There is another aspect which I hope will be discussed this afternoon. I have the material here to do so but because my time is limited I shall leave it to others. I refer to the matter of the advertising and the sale of vitamins to a gullible Canadian public. I hope that two or three hon. members who are doctors will discuss that matter in full. It seems to me that Canadians are being bilked of millions
Request for Commercial Advertising Survey of dollars every year by this racket, and in my view it is nothing but a racket. If a person has a well balanced diet, and almost everyone in this country knows what a well balanced diet is, there is no need for all these vitamins. They are simply swallowed and the system does not absorb them, but people are spending millions of dollars on them every year.
Dr. Monagle, chief of the nutrition division of the federal health department, discussed this matter fully when he addressed the Canadian fruit wholesalers association. If hon. members are interested in this point I would be most happy to discuss it with them.
There is another racket which we have not yet encountered in Canada but which is very prevalent in the United States. It has to do with fall-out shelters. We can expect the same thing to happen here soon because it seems to me we are on the brink of annihilation unless we learn to live with one another. People are beginning to think of their preservation more than ever. It has been noted that in the United States manufacturers of fall-out shelters have been using the fear of people in order to mislead them. I have here a list of 15 different actions on the part of U.S. manufacturers of fall-out shelters for which they have been castigated. They include the making of false or misleading statements, false implications, the use of pictures that give a false impression of the product, down payments that are made to appear as the entire price, phony guarantees, false indications of official government endorsement, claims that the product is custom made, bait advertising, sales promotions involving lotteries, scare tactics and so on. These are things that might be used with regard to almost any product one can name. There are many other practical cases but I do not think I have too much time left. The other day in the Ottawa Journal there was a "Brother Juniper" cartoon. I do not know how other members feel about these cartoons but I get a great deal of enjoyment out of the little fellow. In this one he is talking to one of the other brothers and he is saying:
How come they're always putting new ingredients into toothpaste? Why don't they just put in toothpaste?
I think that is a very sensible idea.

speechtext: Instead of towels in breakfast food.

speechtext:
Towels in packages of detergents. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) has brought up a good point. Detergent boxes are half filled with towels and boxes of breakfast food are half filled with plastic gimmicks for children. There are a number of other points I should like to make. There is the brain

Request for Commercial Advertising Survey washing that seems to be practised on our children in this day and age by means of advertising. I believe the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Pitman) has that point in mind and plans to speak about it. Then there is the matter of the built-in obsolescence in so many of our products that we buy.
Finally, I want to say a few words about radio and television. They provide great entertainment for us but I think we have some false standards. We all see television programs for which some sick comic or some fellow who cannot sing is paid perhaps $50,000 to appear on a program and sing a song or two. Then the sponsor has to sell a million tubes of toothpaste to pay him. We see that kind of thing going on whereas on the other hand a man who is making some contribution to this world of ours has to work five years to earn that much money.
It also seems to me that on television and radio-I suppose those concerned will not take this comment kindly-there are far too many commercials. They are too loud and too long. If they could somehow or other be compelled to have their commercials only half as loud as the rest of the program instead of twice as loud I think we would be getting somewhere.
I hope other hon. members will contribute to this debate. I am deeply interested in this matter. I believe there is a place for such a committee to investigate and to act as a watchdog with respect to advertising on television and radio, magazine advertising and advertising in some of the newspapers of our country.

speechtext: That is realized.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PREVENT DISTRIBUTION OF MISLEADING INFORMATION
speechtext:
I will try to return the debate to more serious matters, Mr. Speaker. I rise to support the resolution of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae). I think it is a good resolution. I agree with the method of setting up a special committee of this house. I think that the House of Commons should and can be an educational device by means of which we could scrutinize certain aspects of our society which need scrutiny. This is a sensible and moderate solution. There is no precipitous

action suggested-simply a desire to acquire information. If we look below the border, we will see how special congressional committees have done a job in examining crime and various other aspects of American society about which a certain amount of concern is felt.
Then, too, I think this is the right place to be dealing with this matter at the federal level. At one time, of course, we believed that the government had no right to interfere in these matters. Today there are very stringent federal controls in the area of food and drugs to which the hon. member has already referred. We also saw the Combines Investigation Act amended two years ago to include definite control of certain areas. I will not read that as it has already been read. Certainly we in this group have constantly encouraged greater concern by the federal government in this area of advertising. If one reads the record of the banking and commerce committee for 1960, he will find there attempts by members of the C.C.F. group to introduce amendments to the Combines Investigation Act to deal with the problem the hon. member has brought forward.
We are very happy, therefore, to see other political parties are now concerned with this matter of advertising. We are all very greatly impressed with the work of the Canadian association of consumers. They cannot be praised too highly. Of course, it is a private organization and its work is limited by a lack of funds. Advertising is very big business and has no need for more funds. One may look at the general area of advertising and say it has grown out of all proportion to its importance in our society. At one time, advertising was considered to have an informative role; it was to give information about products. Today, with our Madison avenue techniques joining forces with psychology and the hidden persuaders about which we have heard so much, it is a force in our society with which we need to concern ourselves.
Those of us in this house who are concerned about democracy I think must realize that democracy is based upon the ability of men and women to make a free choice. This house must concern itself with any activity that might undermine that freedom of choice. When a medium may be used to divert or damage the kind of democratic society we are creating, then this house certainly has reason to be concerned. We protect people physically from poisons, from bad food, and it may be that we should protect them from mental and spiritual injury as well. Some people may see this as an affront to freedom and say that a man can use his money as he wishes. I say, no. The techniques of modern advertising may very well be a threat to the kind of

society which we in this house are seeking to build. The state must often put on controls to protect that freedom.
We have talked a great deal about freedom of the individual, and this is an area in which we can protect that freedom. Today, of course, advertising has become more and more complex. It was very easy to tell the various types of textiles in the early days. They were either wool or cotton. Today, however, with the synthetic textiles like dacron, nylon and so on, it is very difficult to identify these textiles and the public can be easily misled. I think, therefore, this is a very important resolution, and one which should receive the attention and concern of this house. I do not think I need to indicate the number of areas in which we have seen false and misleading advertising. We have seen it, perhaps, in its most pernicious form, in the area where our young children are concerned. We have seen television programs containing advertising designed to give young children certain ideas by means of which they can put pressure upon their parents. We have seen various methods by which the young people of our country have been used in order to create future markets for these particular products.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury mentioned the whole area of fallout shelters. One could mention a lot of other areas as well, such as toothpaste and cigarettes in which the advertising has been misleading and false. Finance companies which advertise the advantages of borrowing from this company as compared to that are certainly not in any sense guided by the truth. We agree that most of the manufacturers and retailers in this country do not need to be controlled by this kind of legislation. However, there are always a few and, in a sense, we have to protect the ethical businessman from the unethical businessman with this kind of legislation.
I do not wish to take up any more time. There are other members who wish to speak. In conclusion, I would say that all parties here are concerned with the individual and the sanctity of the personality. The first problem is the use in advertising of such words as, "most doctors recommend"; or, "three out of four baseball players use"; or, "four out of five housewives prefer". This is the sort of advertising which appears to be making a factual statement but, none the less, to the uninitiated, will have its appeal.
Then, may I turn to the second problem which is connected with advertising in the visual field. I am thinking of recent golf matches which a television crew had tried to cover in some far-off part of the world. The crew came back but found that part of their film was missing. They had to take the star out to simulate some of the shots. This, of course, was in the realm of fiction, although it really did not alter the outcome of that particular golf match.
Then, the third problem is the T.V. actor who sips coloured water instead of whisky, which is probably to his advantage.
The fourth problem is the quality of detergents, in which shirts are shown whiter than white, or whiter than brand X washed shirts, and sometimes you find that these are actually blue shirts because on television blue shirts photograph whiter than white shirts. Still another problem arises from the food freezer scheme.
A further problem which arose in the United States very recently concerned a shoe company which said its shoes would correct, prevent and relieve a large variety of ailments. I list some of them as indigestion, stomach ulcers, high blood pressure and arthritis, which is quite a claim for any shoe company to make. However, it was persuaded to tone down these rather high-flown claims to a simple statement that its shoes would give relief only for hip pains, swollen joints and ankles.

Yet another type of problem arose very recently when one large company was giving away a fruit bowl as one of its premiums. It stated that if you sent in so many box tops, or what have you, you would receive this very large glass bowl for holding fruit. It was actually an eight inch bowl which would not hold many bananas, apples, grapefruit or oranges, but the advertising agency substituted a 12 inch glass bowl in its pictures which, of course, would hold that much more fruit and bring that many more suckers into the field to obtain that type of bowl.
Then there is the puzzling case of the advertiser who was left speechless. This was the Gillette Safety Razor Company, to which we all owe a debt in the fall of the year when they bring us the world series. It had been seeking the superior razor blade and, by golly, it did turn up with the superior razor blade, one that could live up to just about any claim you could make for long life and the quality of shave it gave. The company looked hard for words to describe this marvel but over the years it had already used all the words in the English dictionary to describe less superior products.

The company finally settled on a simple statement that their new blade was indeed the best for shaving.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae) mentioned that I would probably be dealing with a recent case in the United States involving the Colgate-Palmolive Company which was found guilty of misrepresenting a rapid shaving cream. Perhaps most of us have seen the television commercials already. The cream is applied to sandpaper and then the whole thing wiped off very quickly. However, in actual fact the federal trade commission in the United States found that the purported sandpaper was a sheet of plexiglass to which sand had been applied. Some of the reasoning in their judgment is of extreme interest to this debate initiated by my hon, friend, and so I would like to put it on record. This was a unanimous ruling by the federal trade commission and the gist of the ruling was that television camera trickery must not be used in demonstrating the qualities of a product offered for sale. The ruling accompanied a commission order against Colgate-Palmolive Co., and its advertising agency, Bates and Company, Inc., of New York city, prohibiting them from falsely advertising shaving cream, and from using spurious or false mockups or demonstrations for any product. The commission declared:
The limitations of the television medium may present a challenge to the creative ingenuity of

copywriters; but surely they do not constitute lawful justification for resort to falsehoods and deception of the public. Any argument to the contrary would seem to be based on the wholly untenable assumption that the primary function of television is to sell goods, and that the commission should not make any ruling which would impair the ability of sponsors and agencies to use television with maximum effectiveness as a sales or advertising medium.
Stripped of polite verbiage, the argument boils down to this: where truth and television salesmanship collide, the former must give way to the latter. This is obviously an indefensible proposition. The notion that a sponsor may take liberties with the truth in its television advertising, while advertisers using other media must continue to be truthful, is patent nonsense. The statutory requirements of truth in advertising apply to television no less than to other media of communication-
In this case the pictorial test of Rapid Shave, proving to any doubting Thomas in the vast audience that "it really could shave sandpaper" was the clinching argument made by the commercials. The "sandpaper test" was conducted as the announcer said, "to prove Rapid Shave's super moisturizing power..." without this visible proof of its qualities, some viewers might not have been persuaded to buy the product. At least, Colgate-Palmolive must have thought so, or else they would not have emphasized the pictorial "sandpaper test" in the expensive television advertisements of their product.
Finally, in this decision of the federal trade commission comes:
One need only consider the difference in the impact of these commercials on viewers had they been told, honestly and truthfully, that what they were seeing tested was a plexiglass mock-up, rather than what they thought and were told they were seeing, namely, actual sandpaper. The difference between telling and not telling the truth, could, in this instance at least, have been the difference between an effective and ineffective "sell". In such circumstances, the claim of "harmless exaggeration" is rather hollow.
I shall leave the record with that very brief statement on the principles applied by the federal trade commission, not only quoted from the standpoint of the grounds of the decision but also to show a little bit of the philosophy that can be brought into this field.
Some hon. members have already suggested that it may be said against the hon. member for York-Sunbury that he has attempted to interfere with the freedom of the press. On that point I would like to say that I do not believe freedom of the press is a licence of the press to be irresponsible. As I conceive it, it is the duty of the press to act within reasonable and civilized limits and not to accept any philosophy which would allow certain people, advertisers for example, to use the press to peddle untruths and half truths which may either be very damaging or partly damaging to the public. However, I do not say that in all the cases I have mentioned one should consider taking action against the advertisers.
In health matters, yes. I think it would be a good idea if the committee envisaged by the hon. member for York-Sunbury could

look at the regulations now dealing with food, drugs and medicines, because these are basic to health and perhaps the present regulations are not strict enough. I think we might also have a look at advertising in connection with many matters. We might also have a look at the problem to see whether sections of the Criminal Code dealing with fraud are strong enough.
Over-all, sir, I would support the resolution. I think its spirit is a sound one and I also think it would be welcomed by the vast majority of publishers, the vast majority of people in television and radio, and probably even by the vast majority of advertising agencies themselves. The honest advertising agency is caught in this position; if he does not stoop to the odd bit of chicanery himself, his unscrupulous rivals, who might stoop to photographing a blue shirt to prove that is whiter than the white shirt, will simply pass him by in the race for the consumer's dollar. There is one other matter I wish to mention in connection with this resolution. I wish to place this information on the record in the hope that when Hansard leaves the printing presses and is distributed across the country to the various universities, some mathematicians either in our university communities or perhaps within the government service itself may help in solving a problem which is related to advertising. This is a problem which has baffled me as it has baffled a lot of people who have attempted to find some way in which a person borrowing money and embarking on credit arrangements can determine the annual rate of interest from the pattern of payments and make a fair evaluation as against other sources of credit available to him in our economy.

But the request I should like to put forward is this; I hope that some talented mathematician may resolve it for us. This formula gives the precise interest rate as an annual rate, but I would be satisfied with a much simpler formula which would arrive at the annual interest rate, give or take 1 or 2 per cent. Having found such a formula, a much simpler one than the one I have just put on record, the next step would be to have some ingenious person evolve a simple arithmetical calculator which would quickly produce the interest rate being charged. I have in mind a simple type of computer such as hon. members will have seen used for other purposes. I am hopeful that once the initial work and calculations had been carried out this device could be made out of heavy cardboard or plastic- something which would not involve much expense and something which could be made readily available to every person who has dealings in credit. Then we would have a situation where a person embarking on a small loan or embarking on a purchasing program on a credit basis would be able to tell what the annual interest rate involved in the transaction would be. He would then have a freedom of choice which, I suggest, should be an important ingredient in every shopper's activities, to decide whether it might be better to purchase the item he has in mind through the scheme before him or through some other form of credit, for example, a bank, a small loan company or some other source.
I hope, this problem having been placed on record in Hansard and going out, as it will, to the universities and many other circles in our country, that some bright

mathematician may be able to assist this parliament and this country in finding a solution to a problem which has escaped serious investigation for some time.
